expected_evidence: geological: a widespread ~12,900 cal BP (~10,950 BCE) 'Younger Dryas boundary' sedimentary layer containing platinum and iridium anomalies, magnetic and glassy microspherules, nanodiamonds, and a soot/char 'black mat' horizon across multiple North American (and some global) sites
material/archaeological: abrupt discontinuity or thinning in Clovis-culture artifact density and megafauna bone assemblages at ~10,950 BCE, burn layers or charcoal spikes at contemporaneous sites
genetic: population bottleneck signatures in North American megafauna (mammoth, horse, etc.) lineages dated to the YD onset; weaker/less certain bottleneck signal in Paleoindian human mtDNA/Y-DNA

astronomical/geological: absence or near-absence of a confirmed impact crater of appropriate age (expected under an airburst-only mechanism, so this is a predicted non-finding rather than contrary evidence)
oral_tradition: possible (highly speculative) deep-time Native American flood/fire/'sky-fire' origin narratives sometimes invoked as folk-memory of the event (model-prior, very low confidence)
iconographic: none expected (no symbolic/artistic tradition in the region capable of recording such an event at this time)
textual: none possible (pre-literate period and region)
response.rationale: The hypothesis matches the well-known 'Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis' (Firestone et al. 2007 and successors), which I recognize primarily from training as model-prior — I flag it as such rather than established fact, since it remains scientifically contested. If a cosmic airburst near 10,950 BCE triggered YD cooling, the primary expected signature is geological/sedimentological (platinum/iridium spikes, microspherules, nanodiamonds, black mats), which the table rates at 0.65 detectability for the younger-dryas period — sediment and ice-core layers from this era are known to survive over millennia and have in fact been sampled extensively, so this evidence class is both plausible to expect and plausible to have been found (and claims of such findings do exist, though disputed as to cause). Material/archaeological evidence (0.35) is moderately detectable — Clovis-site discontinuities have been documented, though attribution to an impact versus other causes (over-hunting, climate) is ambiguous. Genetic evidence (0.30) for megafaunal bottlenecks is plausible but coarse-grained given the resolution of ancient DNA dating at this timescale. Astronomical evidence in the direct sense (observational/crater) is essentially undetectable by definition of an airburst mechanism (no crater expected), so the table's high 0.70 astronomical score is somewhat misleading for this specific mechanism — I discount it substantially. Textual (0.0) and iconographic (0.10) evidence are essentially impossible given the absence of writing and limited symbolic material culture in Paleoindian North America. Oral tradition (0.10) is too temporally distant (127+ centuries) for any narrative to survive with fidelity; any claimed correspondences are almost certainly model-prior speculation, not verifiable evidence. Given that some proponents claim to have found the predicted geological markers while critics dispute the interpretation (attributing spherules/nanodiamonds to wildfires, volcanism, or terrestrial processes), the overall situation is one of contested-but-existing evidence rather than absence-due-to-non-detectability. I therefore do not think a low detectability score should be invoked to explain away silence — evidence has been actively searched for and reported, just interpreted differently by different researchers. My suggested overall detectability adjustment (0.5) reflects a moderate, mixed picture: strong geological/material search potential, but weak-to-absent astronomical, textual, iconographic, and oral-tradition corroboration inherent to the period and mechanism, and unresolved interpretive disputes over the existing physical evidence.
